**No.** The story stays inside a single first-person consciousness: an unemployed, idle narrator who follows two strangers home and watches them through their window.

- **The narrator is convincing.** His self-deceptions ("I told myself I was going the same way," "I told myself I was waiting out the rain") quietly expose the voyeuristic, morally questionable side of his behavior. That interiority is believable and consistent.
- **No other perspective is offered.** The couple stay opaque. They are seen only from outside and serve as symbolic mirrors of the burned chair, not as minds the story explores. No one else gets a viewpoint either, so there is no real diversity of perspectives.
- **The unlikeable side is underplayed.** The narrator's intrusiveness is framed more as a lyrical "affliction" than examined as something troubling. The story doesn't really challenge the reader with a difficult or objectionable mindset.
